relationship: Refusal of the company of evildoers
rationale: The blessed person refuses the counsel, way and seat of the ungodly. Psalm 25 likewise refuses to sit with an empty council or the ungodly and rejects an assembly of evildoers; the shared concern is chosen association with wrongdoing.

relationship: Meditation on the law day and night
rationale: Both texts describe meditation on the law day and night. Joshua connects this discipline with doing what is written and prospering, while the psalm makes delight in the Lord's law the blessed person's defining practice.

relationship: Watered tree and continuing fruitfulness
rationale: The psalm compares the blessed person to a tree beside waters, bearing seasonal fruit without losing its leaf. Jeremiah compares the person trusting the Lord to a tree beside waters that continues bearing fruit through heat and drought.

relationship: Wind-scattered plant matter and the wicked
rationale: The psalm pictures the ungodly as chaff flung away by wind. In Job's discussion of the wicked, they are compared with straw before wind and dust swept by a storm; the shared image is instability and dispersal, within different arguments about their fate.

relationship: Exclusion of the evil from the righteous in judgment
rationale: The psalm excludes the ungodly from judgment and sinners from the righteous council. Jesus' explanation of the net separates the evil from the righteous at the age's consummation. This compares exclusion in judgment without turning the psalm's wording into a separate claim about resurrection.

relationship: Known righteous ways and the perishing of sinners
rationale: Psalm 1 contrasts the Lord's knowledge of the righteous way with the perishing of the ungodly way. Psalm 36 says the Lord knows the ways of the blameless and contrasts their enduring inheritance with sinners who perish.

relationship: Quotation of the raging nations
rationale: The gathered believers quote the question about raging nations and peoples devising empty things, attributing it to God's speech through David. Their surrounding prayer applies the quoted opposition to the gathering against Jesus.

relationship: Quotation applied to opposition against Jesus
rationale: Acts quotes the kings and rulers gathering against the Lord and His Christ, then names Herod, Pontius Pilate, Gentiles and Israel's peoples as gathering against God's anointed Servant Jesus. The target itself supplies that application.

relationship: Rebellion pictured as broken yoke and bonds
rationale: The rebellious speakers propose tearing bonds and casting away a yoke. Jeremiah describes those who recognized the Lord's way nevertheless breaking the yoke and tearing the bonds together. The images of rejected restraint match, although Jeremiah addresses a different group.

relationship: The Lord's laughter at hostile nations
rationale: The heavenly Lord laughs and sneers at the rebels in Psalm 2. Psalm 58 likewise says the Lord will laugh them to scorn and reduce nations to nothing, presenting divine contempt for threatening opponents rather than fear of their power.

relationship: Divine anger confronting kings and nations
rationale: The Lord's angry speech troubles the rulers who oppose Him in Psalm 2. Psalm 109 describes the Lord crushing kings on the day of His anger and judging among nations. The comparison concerns royal opposition subjected to divine anger, without identifying a single narrated battle.

relationship: Zion and kingship established by the Lord
rationale: The appointed king speaks of Zion as God's holy mountain. The narrative joins David's capture and residence in Zion with his recognition that the Lord prepared him as king. This supplies a concrete Davidic royal setting without identifying the psalm with that precise occasion.

relationship: Explicit citation of the second psalm
rationale: Acts explicitly names the second psalm and quotes the decree about the Son begotten today in its announcement that God fulfilled the fathers' promise by raising Jesus. The reference and its application are stated in the target itself.

relationship: Sonship decree in the comparison with angels
rationale: Hebrews quotes the Lord's declaration of sonship and begetting today while asking which angel ever received such speech. The royal decree is used in the target's argument concerning the Son's distinction from angels.

relationship: Sonship decree and the calling of Christ
rationale: Hebrews quotes the decree about sonship and begetting today when explaining that Christ did not glorify Himself to become high priest. Its context joins the quoted declaration to divine calling, rather than self-assumed honor.

relationship: Granted authority over nations
rationale: The son is promised nations as an inheritance and the earth's ends as a possession. Daniel's vision describes authority given to the figure of the preceding verse and worship by all the earth's nations. Both portray worldwide dominion as granted, without forcing the two passages' figures into an independently established identity.

relationship: Judgment as the shattering of pottery
rationale: The nations are to be crushed like a potter's vessel. Isaiah compares the coming collapse to an earthen vessel shattered beyond useful fragments. The particular comparison is the destructive pottery image; Isaiah's warning concerns its own disobedient audience.

relationship: Kings and judges summoned to understand
rationale: Both texts directly call kings to understand and the earth's judges to receive instruction. Wisdom explains that their authority comes from the Lord and that He will examine their actions, developing the accountability implicit in the psalm's warning.

relationship: Service to God with reverent fear
rationale: The psalm commands service to the Lord with fear and rejoicing with trembling. Hebrews urges acceptable service with reverence and awe, adjoining the warning that God is a consuming fire. Both join worship with serious awareness of divine judgment.

relationship: Instruction accepted or rejected and contrasting outcomes
rationale: The psalm commands taking hold of instruction, warning of anger and perishing while blessing those who trust. Wisdom's speech contrasts refusal of counsel and fear of the Lord with the hopeful, secure dwelling of the one who listens. The connection preserves the psalm's actual instruction wording.

relationship: Named historical setting of flight from Absalom
rationale: The title places David's psalm during flight from his son Absalom. The narrative reports Israel's support for Absalom and David's command to flee Jerusalem, followed by his departure with his household; it directly supplies the setting named by the title.

relationship: Increasing opposition in Absalom's conspiracy
rationale: The speaker laments multiplied afflicters and many rising against him. In the Absalom setting specified by the title, the narrative expressly says the conspiracy strengthened and the people with Absalom increased, before the report that Israel's hearts followed him.

relationship: Hostile interpretation of David's calamity
rationale: The psalm reports claims that God offers the speaker no salvation. During David's flight, Shimei interprets his calamity and Absalom's kingship as the Lord's repayment, while David still hopes for the Lord's favor. This compares the hostile theological accusation without identifying the psalm's many speakers solely with Shimei.

relationship: Divine help and the raising of the head
rationale: Psalm 3 calls the Lord its helper and the one who lifts the speaker's head. Psalm 26 describes God's shelter and the raising of the speaker's head above enemies, making lifted head imagery an expression of protection and restored standing.

relationship: The cry heard from the holy dwelling
rationale: The speaker's voiced cry is heard from the Lord's holy mountain. Psalm 17 likewise recounts a distressed cry whose voice God hears from His holy temple. Both locate the answering of the afflicted worshipper's voice at God's holy dwelling.

relationship: Trust expressed through lying down and sleeping
rationale: Psalm 3 recounts lying down, sleeping and awakening because of the Lord's help. Psalm 4 resolves to lie down and sleep in peace because the Lord grants hopeful dwelling. Sleep becomes a concrete expression of dependence on divine protection.

relationship: Fearlessness before an encircling force
rationale: Psalm 3 refuses fear of tens of thousands attacking on every side. Psalm 26 similarly refuses fear even if an army deploys and war rises against the speaker. The shared affirmation specifically concerns military encirclement or attack.

relationship: God breaking the teeth of enemies
rationale: The appeal for rescue recalls God crushing sinners' teeth. Psalm 57 says God shattered their teeth and crushed lions' grinders. Both use broken teeth to represent the disabling of threatening wicked power.

relationship: Deliverance assigned to the Lord
rationale: Psalm 3 declares that salvation belongs to the Lord and blesses His people. Jonah's vow of praise and thanksgiving ends by assigning deliverance to the Lord. The concluding attribution places rescue with God rather than the endangered worshipper.

relationship: Room granted in response to a distressed call
rationale: The speaker recalls being heard and given room in affliction. Psalm 117 similarly says that a call made in affliction was answered with room to breathe. The repeated contrast of constriction and enlarged space describes answered distress.

relationship: Vanity and falsehood as misdirected attachment
rationale: The psalm challenges love of vanity and pursuit of falsehood. Jonah contrasts those guarding vain and false things with his own thanksgiving, saying they abandoned their mercy. Both reject attachment to vanity and falsehood as a spiritual misdirection.

relationship: Reuse of the command about anger without sin
rationale: Ephesians repeats the psalm's command to be angry and not sin, adding that anger must not outlast the sunset or give room to the devil. The psalm's own continuation directs inward speech and remorse on the bed; the applications remain distinct.

relationship: Righteous sacrifice and the worshipper's inner response
rationale: Psalm 4 calls for righteous sacrifice after its instruction about inward remorse. Psalm 50 joins the broken and humbled heart with anticipated delight in a sacrifice of righteousness. The comparison concerns rightly offered sacrifice in a setting of inward correction.

relationship: The favorable light of the Lord's face
rationale: The psalm answers the demand for good things with the light of the Lord's face marked upon the people. The priestly blessing asks that His face shine upon Israel with mercy and be lifted toward them in peace. Both express divine favor through the face's light.

relationship: Increase of grain, wine and oil
rationale: The psalm joins God-given gladness with a season of increased grain, wine and oil. Deuteronomy names the same three products among the land's fruit blessed by God. The connection is this agricultural blessing, without rewriting the psalm as a comparison saying joy exceeds harvest wealth.

relationship: Peaceful sleep grounded in divine help
rationale: The speaker will lie down and sleep in peace because of the Lord's hopeful provision. Psalm 3 recounts lying down, sleeping and awakening because the Lord helps. Both connect ordinary vulnerable sleep with trust in God's care.

relationship: Morning prayer reaching the Lord
rationale: Psalm 5 expects the Lord to hear in the morning while the speaker stands and watches. Psalm 87 likewise says that the morning prayer will reach the Lord first. The parallel concerns the deliberate presentation of prayer at morning.

relationship: Moral conditions of dwelling with God
rationale: Psalm 5 denies that an evildoer can sojourn with God. Psalm 14 asks who may sojourn in God's dwelling and answers with blameless conduct, righteousness, truthful speech and refusal of harm. The two formulations give negative and positive accounts of access to the holy dwelling.

relationship: Wrongdoing excluded from the speaker's sight and house
rationale: Psalm 5 says the lawless cannot remain before God's eyes. In Psalm 100 the Davidic speaker refuses lawlessness before his eyes and says an unjust speaker did not prosper before them. The comparison joins moral exclusion and the eyes image while distinguishing God from the human householder who addresses Him.

relationship: Falsehood and bloodshed among what the Lord hates
rationale: Psalm 5 joins destruction of false speakers with the Lord's abhorrence of bloodshed and deceit. Proverbs' description of what the Lord hates includes an unjust tongue, hands shedding righteous blood and a witness kindling falsehoods. The paired speech and bloodshed offenses give the connection its particular content.

relationship: Bowing toward the holy temple in response to mercy
rationale: Psalm 5 anticipates entering God's house through abundant mercy and bowing toward His holy temple. Psalm 137 likewise bows toward the holy temple and thanks God's name for mercy and truth. Worship directed toward the temple is expressly joined to mercy in both.

relationship: Guidance on the upright way because of enemies
rationale: Psalm 5 asks for guidance in righteousness and a straight divine way because of enemies. Psalm 26 asks for instruction in God's way and guidance on an upright path for the same stated reason. Both requests link moral direction to hostile pressure.

relationship: Quotation of the open tomb and deceitful tongues
rationale: Romans repeats the throat as an opened tomb and the tongues practicing deceit in its collection of scriptural accusations of sin. The psalm supplies these particular images of corrupt speech; Romans applies the collected testimony to its wider argument about Jews and Greeks under sin.

relationship: Prayer that hostile counsel fail
rationale: Psalm 5 asks that opponents fall away from their counsels. David's response to Ahithophel's joining Absalom is a prayer that the Lord scatter his counsel. The narrative illustrates a particular prayer against hostile planning without fixing Psalm 5 to that event.

relationship: Hope in the divine name expressed as rejoicing
rationale: Psalm 5 joins the rejoicing of those hoping in God with the boasting of those loving His name. Psalm 32 likewise joins the heart's rejoicing in Him with hope in His holy name and a prayer for mercy. The combined name, hope and joy language connects the worshippers' response.

relationship: Shared heading concerning the eighth
rationale: Both headings identify a Davidic psalm for the end and specify concerning the eighth; Psalm 6 additionally mentions hymns. The connection records the distinctive repeated heading without deciding whether the eighth denotes an instrument, musical arrangement or another referent.

relationship: Repeated plea against rebuke in divine anger
rationale: Psalm 37 repeats the complete plea not to be rebuked in God's fury or disciplined in His anger. The identical paired petitions connect the laments without making their surrounding illness descriptions a single historical incident.

relationship: Troubled bones and the need for healing
rationale: Psalm 6 asks for mercy and healing because the speaker is weak and the bones are troubled. Psalm 37 speaks of no healing in the flesh and no peace for the bones, there explicitly relating the condition to anger and sins. The physical language matches while the fuller explanations remain distinct.

relationship: The troubled soul addressed to God
rationale: The psalm's greatly troubled soul turns to the Lord with a question of delay. Jesus likewise speaks of His troubled soul and addresses the Father concerning the approaching hour and the Father's name. This compares the voiced anguish and prayer, without identifying the psalmist's occasion with Jesus' hour.

relationship: Death and Hades contrasted with living praise
rationale: Psalm 6 asks who will remember or thank God in death and Hades. Hezekiah's prayer says those in Hades do not praise and contrasts them with the living who bless God. Both use that contrast within a plea or thanksgiving concerning endangered life.

relationship: Tears occupying the sufferer's nights
rationale: Psalm 6 pictures the bed and resting place soaked by tears every night. Psalm 41 makes tears the speaker's bread day and night amid questioning about God. Both render prolonged grief through bodily images of tears filling ordinary daily life.

relationship: Eye troubled with anger amid enemies
rationale: Psalm 6 describes an eye troubled from anger and aging among enemies. Psalm 30 likewise describes the eye troubled with anger, then failing years, groaning and reproach among enemies. The unusual eye-and-anger expression is accompanied by closely related affliction language.

relationship: Dismissal of workers of lawlessness
rationale: The psalm tells all workers of lawlessness to stand away because the Lord has heard the weeping. Jesus' judgment saying likewise dismisses those practicing lawlessness. The shared dismissal is preserved while its grounds differ: answered lament here and Jesus' refusal to recognize the claimants there.

relationship: Appeal to God for rescue from a pursuer
rationale: Psalm 7 asks God to save and rescue the speaker from pursuers. David addresses Saul's pursuit and asks the Lord to judge his case and give judgment from Saul's hand. The comparison concerns entrusting rescue from pursuit to God, without identifying Psalm 7's unnamed pursuers as Saul.

relationship: A lion-like enemy and the appeal for rescue
rationale: Psalm 7 fears seizure of the soul like a lion when no rescuer is present. Psalm 16 describes enemies taking the speaker up like a hunting lion and immediately asks the Lord to arise and rescue the soul. The predator image and rescue request form the particular parallel.

relationship: Conditional innocence oath before divine judgment
rationale: Psalm 7 begins a conditional acknowledgment of wrongdoing that leads to a self-directed curse in its following verses. Job likewise sets out possible misconduct, appeals to God's righteous weighing and accepts loss if guilty. The comparison is the conditional oath form, not an identification of the offenses or speakers.

relationship: Refusal to repay an enemy's evil in kind
rationale: Psalm 7 makes repayment of evil to those who repay evil a condition of its self-curse. Saul acknowledges that David repaid his evil with good by sparing him. The narrative gives a concrete nonretaliation comparison while leaving the psalm's occasion unidentified.

relationship: Arise invocation against enemies
rationale: Psalm 7 calls on the Lord to rise in anger within the enemies' boundaries. Moses' invocation when the ark sets out likewise calls on the Lord to arise and scatter His enemies. Both invoke divine action against opposition, in distinct prayer and wilderness settings.

relationship: Request for judgment according to innocence
rationale: Psalm 7 asks the Lord to judge according to the speaker's righteousness and innocence. Psalm 25 likewise requests judgment on the ground of an innocent walk and invites testing of kidneys and heart. The comparison concerns a personal appeal for examination and vindication.

relationship: Righteous judgment testing hearts and kidneys
rationale: Psalm 7 names God as the tester of hearts and kidneys while asking an end to wickedness and direction for the righteous. Jeremiah likewise addresses the just judge who tests kidneys and hearts while entrusting his claim against plotters to Him. Both link inward testing with just adjudication.

relationship: Divine patience alongside justice
rationale: Psalm 7 calls God a righteous, strong and patient judge who does not bring wrath every day. The proclamation in Exodus calls Him slow to anger and merciful while also preserving righteousness and not cleansing the guilty. Patience is joined to, rather than substituted for, judgment.

relationship: Divine sword prepared for judgment
rationale: Psalm 7 warns of God's polished sword if the addressed person does not return. The song in Deuteronomy describes God sharpening His sword as lightning and taking hold of judgment to repay enemies. Both picture threatened judgment as divine preparation of a blade.

relationship: Divine arrows as instruments of deadly judgment
rationale: Psalm 7 describes prepared instruments of death and arrows fashioned for those being burned. Deuteronomy makes God's arrows drunk with blood in vengeance upon enemies. The connection is the deadly divine archery image, without changing Psalm 7 into a statement that its arrows themselves burn.

relationship: Wrongdoing pictured as conception and birth
rationale: The psalm portrays labor with injustice, conception of trouble and birth of lawlessness. Eliphaz pictures conception of pains and a belly bearing deceit. Both give wrongdoing a gestational image; this comparison does not endorse Eliphaz's application of his speech to Job.

relationship: The digger falling into his own pit
rationale: Psalm 7 says the one who excavates a pit will fall into the hole he made. Proverbs likewise says the person digging a pit for a neighbor falls into it. The trap reverses upon its maker in both formulations.

relationship: Attempted harm returning upon its author
rationale: The psalm says trouble returns upon the wrongdoer's head and injustice descends upon his crown. Esther's festival explanation says the evils Haman attempted against the Jews came upon him. The narrative illustrates reversal of intended harm without claiming that it uses the psalm's head imagery.

relationship: Shared heading concerning the winepresses
rationale: Both psalms are marked for the end and concerning the winepresses, while one is Davidic and the other is for Asaph. The distinctive heading is shared without equating authors or settling what winepresses denotes in these headings.

relationship: Worldwide praise and glory above the heavens
rationale: Psalm 8 joins the Lord's wondrous name throughout the earth with magnificence above the heavens. Psalm 112 calls for praise of His name across the sun's course and declares Him above nations with glory above the heavens. Both move from worldwide praise to heavenly exaltation.

relationship: Explicit quotation defending children's praise
rationale: Jesus answers objections to children praising Him in the temple by quoting the preparation of praise from infants and nursing children. Matthew therefore provides an explicit use of this psalmic statement in defense of the children's acclamation.

relationship: The heavenly lights as God's creative work
rationale: The psalm looks at the heavens, moon and stars as works of God's fingers that He founded. Genesis recounts God's making and placing of the heavenly lights and stars. The connection concerns the same created celestial objects, with poetic finger imagery specific to the psalm.

relationship: Quotation of the question about humanity
rationale: Hebrews quotes the question asking what a human being or son of man is that God remembers and cares for him. The citation introduces the target's discussion of subjection and of Jesus in the following verses; that later interpretation is not supplied merely by the phrase son of man alone.

relationship: Human smallness and divine attention in contrasting prayers
rationale: Psalm 8 asks why God remembers and visits a human being in a context of bestowed honor. Job similarly asks what a human being is that God magnifies and visits him, but his surrounding plea seeks relief from scrutiny. The shared question serves contrasting responses to divine attention.

relationship: Quotation of lower-than-angels status and crowning
rationale: Hebrews quotes being made a little lower than angels and crowned with glory and honor, then applies that language to Jesus and His suffering of death. The actual angels wording is retained in both passages, while the target supplies its christological use.

relationship: Quotation and exposition of subjection beneath the feet
rationale: Hebrews quotes all things subjected beneath the feet and explains the comprehensiveness of that subjection while acknowledging it is not yet wholly seen. The psalm's grant over God's handiwork is therefore directly reused and interpreted in the target.

relationship: All-things subjection in the resurrection argument
rationale: Paul invokes the subjection of all things beneath His feet, explicitly excepts the One who subjects them and describes the Son's eventual subjection. The psalmic wording is used within a particular account of Christ's reign and its consummation.

relationship: Human rule including cattle and land creatures
rationale: The psalm lists sheep, cattle and animals of the plain under the human figure's granted rule. Genesis' creation declaration gives humankind rule including cattle and the earth's creatures. The shared content is the grant over animal life, not a claim that the two lists have identical wording.

relationship: Human rule over sea fish and heavenly birds
rationale: Psalm 8 includes birds of heaven and fish of the sea among what is subjected to humanity. Genesis' blessing explicitly commands rule over fish of the sea and birds of heaven. The two named classes correspond directly.

relationship: same-chapter opening and closing acclamation
rationale: The psalm ends by repeating the address Lord our Lord and the acclamation that His name is wondrous throughout the earth from its opening praise. This repeated frame encloses the reflection on heavenly creation and the place granted to humankind.

relationship: Thanksgiving joined to recounting all God's wonders
rationale: Psalm 9 promises wholehearted thanks and recounting all God's wonders. Psalm 104 similarly joins thanksgiving with the command to recount all His wonders. The particular link is the combination of grateful worship and comprehensive rehearsal of divine deeds.

relationship: Enemies turning back in response to God
rationale: Psalm 9 describes the enemy turning back and opponents weakening before God. Psalm 55 expects enemies to turn backward on the day the speaker calls upon God. The shared reversal is specifically the retreat of enemies before divine help.

relationship: Judgment expressed as erasure of a people's name
rationale: Psalm 9 recalls rebuked nations and an erased name. In Deuteronomy the Lord threatens to destroy idolatrous Israel and blot out its name from under heaven. The erasure image corresponds, but the threatened Israel and the psalm's nations are distinct, and Moses' subsequent intercession matters to the narrative.

relationship: The divine throne prepared for judgment
rationale: The psalm says the enduring Lord has prepared His throne for judgment. Daniel sees thrones set in place, an Ancient of Days seated and a court assembled with opened books. Both join divine enthronement with the exercise of judgment, while Daniel supplies visionary details absent from the psalm.

relationship: Judging the inhabited world in righteousness
rationale: The psalm declares that God will judge the inhabited world in righteousness. Paul's speech uses the same formulation and specifies a fixed day and an appointed Man whose resurrection gives assurance. The common judgment language is linked without importing those added specifications into the psalm.

relationship: God as refuge and helper in affliction
rationale: Psalm 9 describes the Lord as refuge for the needy and timely helper in distress. Psalm 45 likewise calls God refuge, strength and helper in overwhelming afflictions. The combined refuge-and-helper formulation connects the descriptions of protective aid.

relationship: Announcing the Lord's deeds among nations
rationale: Psalm 9 calls for praise to the Lord dwelling in Zion and proclamation of His deeds among nations. Psalm 104 likewise calls for thanksgiving and announcing His works among nations. The parallel concerns public proclamation of divine acts beyond the worshipping community.

relationship: God hearing bloodshed and calling it to account
rationale: Psalm 9 says the One who calls bloodshed to account remembers the needy cry. God tells Cain that Abel's blood cries from the ground and pronounces a curse in response. The narrative supplies a concrete instance of shed blood being heard and answered by divine judgment.

relationship: Endangered life at the gates of death
rationale: The psalm addresses God as the One raising the speaker from death's gates. Hezekiah describes his threatened remaining years at Hades' gates before recounting restoration. Both use a gateway to death's realm for mortal danger; their surrounding prayers move toward life and praise.

relationship: Rescued life devoted to praise at God's dwelling
rationale: Following rescue from death's gates, the psalmist seeks to proclaim praise at daughter Zion's gates. Hezekiah contrasts living praise with Hades and promises continual blessing before God's house. Both connect preservation of life with renewed public worship at the holy place.

relationship: A concealed trap catching those who laid it
rationale: Psalm 9 says nations become caught by the destruction and trap they prepared. Psalm 34 asks that the concealed snare catch its makers and that they fall into it. The connection is the precise reversal of a hidden trap upon its authors.

relationship: The sinner caught by his own prepared instrument
rationale: Psalm 9 presents the sinner caught in the works of his own hands as a manifestation of judgment. Haman is hung on the tree he prepared for Mordecai. This is a concrete narrative analogy of a deadly preparation returning upon its maker, not an identification of the psalm's sinner.

relationship: Destruction associated with forgetting God
rationale: The psalm consigns sinners and nations forgetting God to Hades. Bildad describes the end of those who forget the Lord and the perishing of the ungodly person's hope. Both connect forgetting God with a ruinous end, without treating Bildad's speech as a verdict on Job or making its imagery identical to Hades.

relationship: same-chapter remembrance contrasted with the oppressor's claim
rationale: The declaration that the poor will not be utterly forgotten directly counters the later oppressor's assertion that God has forgotten and turned away His face. The contrast distinguishes the psalm's assurance from the wicked person's quoted claim.

relationship: Prayer that human strength not prevail before God
rationale: Psalm 9 asks the Lord to arise so that a human being does not grow strong and nations face judgment. Asa similarly asks that no human being prevail against God while confronting a great force. Both subordinate threatening human strength to divine intervention, in different settings.

relationship: same-chapter timely help questioned in the lament
rationale: The question why the Lord stands far away at fitting times in distress recalls the earlier description of Him as helper at fitting times in distress. The repeated phrasing creates a deliberate tension between confessed refuge and experienced absence within this one psalm.

relationship: Moral inversion in praising wrongdoing
rationale: Psalm 9 describes the sinner praised for desire and the unjust person blessed. Proverbs describes those abandoning the law as praising impiety. Both identify praise directed toward wrongdoing as a distortion of moral judgment.

relationship: The sinner acting without God before his view
rationale: Psalm 9 says God is not before the sinner. Psalm 35 describes the lawless person's inward resolve to sin with no fear of God before his eyes, followed by deceit and planned lawlessness. The parallel concerns practical disregard of God, without replacing either text with an explicit denial that God exists.

relationship: The unshaken boast exposed by a contrasting experience
rationale: The sinner claims he will never be shaken or encounter adversity. Psalm 29 recalls the speaker's own prosperous claim never to be shaken, then God's turned face and resulting trouble. The repeated boast is compared while distinguishing the wicked speaker from the worshipper recalling failed confidence.

relationship: Quotation of the mouth's cursing and bitterness
rationale: Romans repeats the mouth full of cursing and bitterness in its scriptural indictment of sin. Psalm 9 supplies those features within the fuller description that also names deceit and trouble under the tongue; Romans' shorter citation does not reproduce every detail.

relationship: Concealed plotting against an innocent person
rationale: Psalm 9 depicts ambush with rich people and a plan to kill an innocent person in hiding. Proverbs voices a criminal invitation to shared bloodshed, unjust concealment of a righteous man and seizure of property. Both expose collective hidden violence, without attributing every proposed motive to the psalm's ambushers.

relationship: The predator image for oppression of the needy
rationale: The psalm compares the lurking captor of a poor man with a lion in its enclosure. Proverbs compares one tyrannizing over a needy nation with a hungry lion and thirsty wolf. The lion image makes oppression of the vulnerable predatory in both texts.

relationship: The oppressor's claim that God does not see
rationale: Psalm 9 quotes the assertion that God has forgotten and turned away His face forever. Psalm 93 places the claim that the Lord will not see after murder of vulnerable people, then rebuts it through the Creator of the eye. Both expose an oppressive confidence in divine inattention.

relationship: same-chapter denial of accountability contradicted by divine remembrance
rationale: The ungodly person's claim that God will not call to account conflicts with the earlier statement that He calls bloodshed to account and remembers the needy. The intrapsalm comparison separates quoted denial from the psalm's own assertion of justice.

relationship: God's care and judgment for the orphan
rationale: Psalm 9 answers the claim of divine inattention by affirming God's perception and help for the orphan. Deuteronomy describes God as executing judgment for the sojourner, orphan and widow. Both place protection of the orphan within God's active justice.

relationship: The breaking of the sinner's arm
rationale: Psalm 9 asks for the sinful and evil man's arm to be crushed. Psalm 36 says sinners' arms will be shattered while the Lord sustains the righteous. Both use the disabled arm to portray the collapse of wicked power.

relationship: Everlasting divine reign and the land of inheritance
rationale: Psalm 9 joins the Lord's endless reign with the nations' removal from His land. The sea song moves from the request to plant the people in God's mountain of inheritance to the declaration of His everlasting reign. Both connect divine kingship with the place belonging to Him, without equating their historical settings.

relationship: Justice for the orphan against oppression
rationale: Psalm 9 describes judgment for orphan and lowly so that human boasting ceases. Deuteronomy prohibits perverting judgment for the orphan and other vulnerable people and recalls Israel's redeemed slavery. The command gives a concrete human obligation corresponding to the psalm's appeal for protective justice.

relationship: Hidden archery against an upright victim
rationale: Psalm 10 depicts sinners preparing bow and arrows to strike the upright in moonless darkness. Psalm 63 likewise depicts a stretched bow and shooting a blameless person in hiding, adjoining sharpened tongues. Both portray concealed attack against uprightness, without deciding that every weapon in Psalm 10 is figurative speech.

relationship: Divine observation of humanity from the heavenly dwelling
rationale: Psalm 10 places the Lord's throne in heaven and describes His eyes examining human beings. Psalm 32 likewise describes Him looking from heaven and His prepared dwelling upon all humanity and understanding their deeds. Heavenly dwelling is joined to intimate human scrutiny in both.

relationship: Participation in wrongdoing as hostility to one's own life
rationale: Psalm 10 says the lover of injustice hates his own soul. Proverbs says the person sharing with a thief hates his own life. Both describe allegiance to wrongdoing as self-directed harm, with theft the target's specific case.

relationship: Judgment pictured as raining fire and sulfur
rationale: Psalm 10 describes traps, fire, sulfur and storm wind rained upon sinners. Genesis narrates the Lord raining sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah. The shared rain-of-fire-and-sulfur image supplies a specific comparison without identifying the psalm's sinners as those cities or equating every listed element.
